newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish cabinet criticises secret files bill.
newsitem.headline: Polish cabinet criticises secret files bill.

text.p: Poland's government on Tuesday criticised a draft law, proposed by a special parliamentary committee, that would open up secret files to unmask former collaborators of the communist-era security police.
The government, dominated by the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) party, backs such a bill in principle.

But it said the proposal, drafted by a cross-party committee including right-wing opposition deputies and due to be debated by parliament this week, could harm security service operations and compromise innocent people.
"The adoption of these regulations would pose a threat to the tasks of the special services," it said in a statement.

The parliamentary committee draft, also supported by many members of the co-ruling Peasant Party (PSL), would set up a special vetting court to probe whether candidates for state posts had been informers during the period of undemocratic rule from 1944 until the fall of communism in 1989.

Candidates for top government, parliamentary, judicial and public media jobs would have to openly declare whether they had been informants of the SB security police or the intelligence and counter-intelligence services, before taking a post.

They would face up to five years in prison, stiff fines and a ban from selected state jobs if the court found they had lied. But a declaration that they had collaborated would not in itself automatically block their way to such posts.
The government said the bill, on which the lower house of parliament is due to vote this week, defined the notion of collaboration too broadly and imprecisely.

It said the measure would harm current security service operations by revealing intelligence and counter-intelligence agents and not just those of the political police which worked to destroy the anti-communist opposition before 1989.
The bill looks set to trigger heated disputes during the run-up to this year's parliamentary elections, but it is unlikely to be adopted in its current shape.
Even if most Peasant deputies turn against their coalition partners, the ex-communists, and help the opposition pass the bill, President Aleksander Kwasniewski is likely to veto it.
Kwasniewski, himself a former communist, has already raised objections to the draft like those of the government.
The Peasants and the opposition together are short of the two-thirds majority needed to overturn a presidential veto.
Poland has failed to unmask former communist security police agents, unlike the Czech Republic and the former East Germany where communist files were opened to the public.

Parties rooted in the Solidarity trade union did not address the problem when they held power until 1993. Most of them said the interior ministry files, unverified and possibly often forged, could embarrass innocent public figures.

The coalition of ex-communists and the Peasant party, a grouping also rooted in the old system, buried the issue after it won elections more than three years ago -- partly to avoid drawing attention to the more unsavoury aspects of the past.
But Kwasniewski changed his mind last year and proposed a bill on vetting after his political colleague, SLD leader Jozef Oleksy, was accused of having spied for Moscow.
Oleksy denied the allegations but resigned as prime minister. Prosecutors later dropped their investigation, calling the evidence against Oleksy flawed and inadequate.
